result:
There's a particular hour—somewhere between three and four in the morning—when the world seems to hold its breath. The refrigerator hums its one-note song. A car passes, occasionally, tires hissing on wet asphalt. And in that hush, thoughts take on a strange clarity, or a strange distortion, depending on the night.

I think about how much of life is spent waiting for things to begin. We treat the ordinary hours as corridors between rooms, something to get through on the way to the anniversary, the promotion, the trip we've been planning. But the corridor is most of the house. The Tuesday afternoons, the dishes, the drive home in fading light—this is the actual fabric, and we rarely notice its weave until some ending forces us to look back and count.

There's a Japanese concept, *mono no aware*, the gentle sadness of things—the awareness of impermanence that makes a cherry blossom more beautiful precisely because it falls. I used to think that was a melancholy idea. Now I think it's a practical one. If nothing lasts, then attention is the only real possession we have. Where we place it is how we spend our lives, whether or not we're paying attention to the spending.

The light is starting to change at the edge of the window. Gray becoming something warmer. A bird tests a note, then commits to a whole phrase. The extraordinary thing is not that the sun rises—astronomers can explain that—but that it rises as if for the first time, and that we get to be here, groggy and unfinished, to see it happen again.
